extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and categorize the phenomenon of self-censorship: its definition, causes (social, economic, legal, taste), sectoral manifestations (media, science), risks (information hazards), and regional examples. Useful for readers studying speech, media freedom, and institutional behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of self-censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-censorship is the act of censoring or classifying one's own discourse, typically out of fear or deference to the perceived preferences, sensibilities, or infallibility of others, and often without overt external pressure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commonly exhibited by film producers, directors, publishers, journalists, musicians, and social media personalities. Contrasted with formal censorship; related to but distinct from legal protections such as Article 19 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights which guarantees freedom of opinion and expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: People withhold or adjust opinions because of fear of social exclusion or unpopularity; shared norms and beliefs can suppress expression to comply or belong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors contributing include gender, age, education, political interests, and media exposure. Example: psychologists' reticence about religious affiliation (APA survey). Concepts like political correctness and the spiral of silence contribute. Survey data (e.g., 2019 German survey) illustrate differences in willingness to speak among friends vs in public or online.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic (market) pressures / soft censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-censorship can occur to conform to market expectations — editors or creators avoid topics that might anger advertisers, customers, or owners to protect livelihood or profitability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sometimes referred to as 'soft censorship'. Applies to media organizations, publishers, and other commercial cultural producers. Organizational incentives (loss of advertising, job risk) drive omission or alteration of content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal / authoritarian pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: In authoritarian countries creators remove material their government might find controversial for fear of sanction by authorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Government policies and potential penalties (jailing, fines, shutdown) are strong drivers of self-censorship; in such contexts self-censorship may be pervasive across media and other sectors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste and decency
rubrics_metrics.description: Curators and editors frequently censor images or material (murder, terrorism, war, massacres) to avoid charges of prurience, shock tactics, or invasion of privacy; children's products may be specially affected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial judgments about audience sensibilities can lead to pre-emptive removal or alteration. Example: museum director whitewashing an antiwar mural to avoid offending the community; relevance to young adult literature and other youth-targeted content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-censorship as a form of preference falsification
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-censorship is a passive form of preference falsification: silence or withholding signals agreement or conceals true preference, while active preference falsification involves asserting the opposite opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes silent suppression from actively stating a contrived opinion. Useful conceptual nuance for analyzing social signaling and collective opinion dynamics (e.g., Kuran's framework).

rubrics_metrics.name: In media (journalists and news organizations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists often censor themselves due to threats, editorial instructions, perceived conflicts of interest with economic sponsors, advertisers, or shareholders; corporate ownership and market forces encourage selection/omission and framing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments (e.g., Manufacturing Consent) posit systematic self-censorship via ownership incentives. Examples include journalists seeking censorship advice from military authorities, suppression of news for safety (NYT abduction story), and advocacy groups raising concerns about internal editorial memos. Self-censorship in media can be a survival strategy to preserve some reporting under threat of crackdown.

rubrics_metrics.name: In science and academia
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-censorship occurs in academia when researchers or editors withhold findings or alter work for political, ideological, or safety reasons; examples include politically-motivated withholding (Nazi-era science) and suppression relating to climate research or endangered species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dual-use research (biology, biotechnology) raises particular concerns; academic self-censorship may stem from institutional pressures, funding dependencies, or fear of reputational/political consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risks from scientific publications / information hazards
rubrics_metrics.description: Some research discoveries pose dual-use risks (e.g., enabling weapons); editors and journal groups recognize that potential harm may outweigh societal benefits and may modify or withhold publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical case: early atomic research highlighted risks; Leo Szilard's arguments. In 2003, leading journal editors agreed to identify safety/security issues and conceded that on occasion a paper should be modified or not published. This is framed as responsible self-censorship to manage information hazards.

rubrics_metrics.name: By region (regional and national manifestations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-censorship manifests differently across countries and regions — examples include widespread practices in China (heavy online pre-moderation, company compliance), Russia (revived practice after 2000s), Turkey (increased with declining press freedoms), various African, Central Asian, European, Latin American, and South Asian contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page documents country- and region-specific drivers (legal threats, market pressures, political intimidation, surveillance) with many case studies and studies cited. Note also cross-border effects (Western companies self-censoring to appease Chinese authorities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational and institutional production of self-censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-censorship can be produced by organizational routines, editorial policies, corporate sponsorship, nonprofit funding, and institutional incentives that shape what is safe or profitable to publish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes internal editorial instructions, memos, and routines that systematically shape selection and omission of stories; organizational survival and institutional norms reinforce self-censoring behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical measurement / survey evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-censorship is measurable via surveys and studies reporting willingness to express views in different contexts and over time (e.g., Allensbach/FAZ German survey: 59% comfortable among friends vs 18% in public; AmeriSpeak/US figures on perceived freedom).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey evidence is used to document prevalence and trends (e.g., reported rise in self-censorship in the US from 13% in 1954 to 46% in 2020 per some studies), though interpretations may vary and be contested.
